newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Chinese Australians face rise in racial abuse - survey.
newsitem.headline: Chinese Australians face rise in racial abuse - survey.

text.p: Racial abuse against Chinese Australians has doubled, with many being spat at or physically threatened, since independent politican Pauline Hanson sparked a xenophobic race debate, according to a Chinese newspaper survey.
The survey in the daily Sing Tao, Australia's largest Chinese language newspaper, released on Wednesday found physical, written and verbal abuse had risen in the past month.

"We had heard of anecdotal reports of more abuse, but the survey showed it had doubled since the speech," said Thiam Ang, president of the Chinese Australian Forum, referring to Hanson's claim that Australia is being swamped by Asians.
"I think it is shameful that law abiding citizens of this country are being attacked because of their appearance. It is a disgraceful thing," Ang told Reuters.
More than 1,000 people responded to the Chinese Australian Forum questionaire in Sing Tao in late October, which asked if, when, and how people had been abused.

One third of respondents, 345 people, said they had experienced abuse before Hanson initiated the race debate in a maiden parliamentary speech on October 12. But 764 people said they had been victimised since the speech.
The survey also asked them to categorise the abuse as physical, written, verbal or whether they had been spat at.
"We had heard a lot of reports that people were being spat on and for Chinese it is a terrible thing. In the Chinese culture it means you are a mongrel dog," Ang said.
The survey found almost a three-fold increase, from 25 to 79, in the number of Chinese Australians being spat on.

The greatest increase in racial abuse was verbal, from 299 to 670. Physical abuse, such as families being pushed around in the street, increased from 40 to 95, while written abuse, such as threatening letters rose from 23 to 47.
"One of the aims of our organisation is to integrate Chinese into Australian society, but this has put us back," Ang said.
Ang said Australian Prime Minister John Howard was wrong when he said recently there had been no increase in abuse against Asian Australians as a result of the race debate.
The Chinese Australian Forum also criticised Howard, saying his failure to end the race debate showed a lack of leadership, a view shared by political analysts and other ethnic groups.
"I think he (Howard) should change his tact and stand up and protect those Australians being hurt -- call on people to stop this abuse," Ang said.
While Howard has said he opposes racial intolerance and does not agree with Hanson, he has championed her right to freedom of speech.
"Many of us grew up in countries where such freedom was curtailed and we appreciate it more than the average Australian who has never had it taken away," Ang said.
"But this freedom of speech does not allow people to abuse people in the street. It is a sad day for Australia when people can't carry out their daily lives without fear of abuse."
Asian Australians make up 4.7 percent of Australia's 18 million population and account for about one third of the country's 100,000 immigrants each year.
Sing Tao has a daily circulation of about 25,000.
